sentences: A monk wrapped in a hood glares out of the picture at us.
He has bulging eyes, heavy brows, a great hooked nose and a thick, bristling beard.
Yet his whole body is made of only a few dark strokes of ink.
This is Bodhidharma, painted by Kim Myeong-guk, a court painter of seventeenth-century Joseon Korea.
The man in the picture is Bodhidharma, the monk said to have travelled from southern India to China and founded Zen Buddhism.
He is famous for the story that he sat facing a cave wall in meditation for nine years.
Zen values sudden insight of the mind over words and scriptures.
We do not even know for certain when Kim Myeong-guk was born or when he died.
He called himself Yeondam, and because he loved drink so much he was also known as Chwiong, the Drunken Old Man.
Several old accounts say he would only take up the brush once he was thoroughly drunk.
He twice travelled to Japan with the Joseon court's diplomatic missions, in 1636 and again in 1643.
For the second mission, it is said, the Japanese side specifically asked for a painter like him.
Some scholars think this picture was painted on one of those two journeys, at the request of someone in Japan.
Now look closely at the face.
The eyes, brows, nose and beard are drawn in paler ink, with relative care.
The furrow between the brows and the upturned eyes give a sense of long, patient concentration.
Then look at the robe.
A brush loaded with dark ink sweeps down from the shoulders in a single movement.
Wherever the brush presses and turns, the ink splits and leaves rough, dry marks.
This way of reducing a figure to the fewest possible strokes is called gampil, or abbreviated brushwork.
In front of the chest, the two hands, hidden in the sleeves, are enclosed by thick, heavy lines.
The delicate face and the bold body meet on the same sheet, and the contrast creates a strange, quiet tension.
Look at the left-hand edge.
There you will find his art name, Yeondam, written in ink, with two red seals stamped below it.
This is where the painter signed the work as his own.
This painting is often named as the most representative Zen painting in Korea.
In Japan at that time, Zen subjects such as Bodhidharma were greatly loved, and Kim's swift, daring brushwork was hugely popular there.
The painting is now in the National Museum of Korea in Seoul.
It is painted in ink alone, on a sheet of paper eighty-three centimetres tall.
Step back and see it whole.
A handful of brushstrokes holds nine years of silent meditation.
Today, try saying something that matters to you in just one sentence, and let the rest stay unspoken.
